title: Teaching Machine Learning in School: A Systematic Mapping of the State of the Art
extended_summary:
This paper asks what instructional units exist for teaching machine learning (ML) concepts in elementary through high school, and what their characteristics are. The authors conduct a systematic mapping study of ML education resources and publications from 2009–2019 to identify and synthesize available instructional units (IUs), the ML concepts they cover, how they are taught, and how they are developed and evaluated.

The study does not test a single intervention; instead, it maps 30 ML instructional units found across articles and online materials. These units include workshops, courses, challenges, tutorials, summer programs, and extracurricular activities, often using block-based programming environments, Python, unplugged activities, or web-based tools. The population spans K-12 learners, with many units aimed at high school and some at elementary/middle school, often beginners with no prior ML experience. The context is mainly school or school-adjacent learning settings, sometimes family-oriented or community-oriented, and many units focus on practical applications such as image classification, robotics, and game-based projects.

The authors conclude that ML education is already appearing in K-12, mostly in recent years, but the field is still immature. Most units emphasize supervised learning, neural networks, and hands-on application, while few address assessment rigorously or provide detailed development/evaluation methods. The paper argues for more systematic instructional design, clearer assessment practices, and better balance between abstracted and explicit ML processes to support meaningful student learning.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic mapping study, but it does not evaluate a ChatGPT-like tool or any direct middle-school mathematics achievement intervention. Its evidence is descriptive and qualitative, summarizing existing K-12 ML instructional units rather than testing learning outcomes against standard instruction.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct empirical impact on middle school mathematics achievement or generative AI use. It provides background mapping of ML education interventions in K-12, but no evidence of effect relative to standard instruction or no AI support.
